title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter
oneLiner: The pressure on bills and on the grid is this decade; a first reactor is the decade after next.
body: The case for repeal is usually made in terms of today's problems: high bills, coal plants closing, a grid under strain. Each of those plays out in the 2020s and 2030s. Even on generous assumptions nothing nuclear would generate before 2040, by which time the coal fleet has closed and the firming it needed has been built from something else.
contextBackground: This is where the live nuclear debate actually sits. Few participants now argue about safety or waste; the argument is about timing. Supporters of repeal say the timeline is an argument for starting now; opponents say it is an argument that nuclear answers a different question from the one being asked. The facts beneath this claim, each argued separately, are the 2040 estimate, the coal closure schedule and the firming already planned with gas.
contextDisagreement: The dates are broadly agreed. The disagreement is whether 'too late for this decade' settles the matter or merely shifts nuclear's role from replacing coal to replacing the gas and first-generation storage that will themselves age out in the 2040s.

evidenceItems.citation: CSIRO and AEMO, GenCost — lead time discussion; AEMO Integrated System Plan — coal retirement and firming

otherClaim.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation

claimItself.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the 1998 prohibition on nuclear power plants should be lifted. Repeal is a separate question from whether anyone would then build one.
claimItself.body: Two federal Acts prohibit the approval of a nuclear power plant anywhere in Australia. Repealing them would allow proposals to be assessed on their merits under the ordinary environmental, safety and planning regimes. Whether a plant would then be commercially viable, or built in time to matter, is argued below.

otherClaim.title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040

claimItself.title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040
claimItself.oneLiner: Legislation, licensing, site selection, workforce and construction each take years, and none has started.
claimItself.body: Starting from no regulator for power reactors, no licensed site and no construction supply chain, the sequence of repeal, regulatory design, licensing, approvals and a first-of-a-kind build is estimated by CSIRO and others at fifteen years or more. On that reckoning a decision taken now delivers first power around 2040 at the earliest.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Australia has no licensing regime, construction supply chain or operating workforce for nuclear power reactors

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: The United Arab Emirates went from deciding to build nuclear power to first grid electricity in about twelve years, with no prior nuclear industry

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: The 2020 independent review of the EPBC Act found its approval processes slow, duplicative and unpredictable

otherClaim.title: Most of the National Electricity Market's remaining coal-fired capacity is scheduled to close by the late 2030s

claimItself.title: Most of the National Electricity Market's remaining coal-fired capacity is scheduled to close by the late 2030s
claimItself.oneLiner: Owners' announced closure dates, and the market operator's planning scenarios, retire the bulk of the coal fleet within fifteen years.
claimItself.body: The Australian Energy Market Operator's Integrated System Plan models the exit of most coal generation across the eastern states during the 2030s, consistent with dates announced by plant owners. Several plants have brought their dates forward rather than back.

otherClaim.title: AEMO's Integrated System Plan relies on gas-fired generation to firm renewables through the 2030s and beyond

claimItself.title: AEMO's Integrated System Plan relies on gas-fired generation to firm renewables through the 2030s and beyond
claimItself.oneLiner: The market operator's own plan keeps gas peakers in the mix as backup, run for a small number of hours a year.
claimItself.body: In every Integrated System Plan scenario, gas-fired peaking plants remain in the system to cover long periods of low wind and solar output. Their capacity is held or grows while their total energy output falls, because they run rarely.
